template:
Hi,

Noticed you do {{business_type}} around {{city}}.

We can book you 10 qualified {{inspection_type}} that turn into paid {{project_type}} jobs, in under 30 days.

You only pay when I book you a qualified, confirmed {{inspection_singular}}.

Open to a 15-minute chat?

instructions.business_type: the trade this company leads with on its own website, lowercase, EXACTLY one of: damp proofing, structural waterproofing, basement waterproofing, underpinning, structural repairs, mini piling, subsidence repair. Use the one the site LEADS with (hero line, page title, the first service listed), not one of many further down. Map what the site actually says onto the seven: rising damp / penetrating damp / condensation and mould / damp and timber / woodworm and dry rot / re-plastering after damp -> damp proofing; tanking / cellar tanking / cavity drainage / Type A or Type C / structural waterproofing -> structural waterproofing; basement waterproofing / basement conversion / cellar conversion -> basement waterproofing; underpinning -> underpinning; crack stitching / wall tie replacement / lateral restraint / masonry and brickwork repair / structural repairs -> structural repairs; mini piling / piling / pile driving / screw piles -> mini piling; subsidence / subsidence repair / heave / movement -> subsidence repair. Never any other phrase, and NEVER 'foundation repair' — that is an American label, it is not what a UK firm calls itself, and it is not in the allowed list.
instructions.inspection_type: the FIRST VISIT to a homeowner, plural, in UK usage: the trade noun for business_type plus that trade's survey/visit word. Take it from this table and change nothing else. damp proofing -> damp surveys; structural waterproofing -> basement surveys; basement waterproofing -> basement surveys; underpinning -> site surveys; structural repairs -> structural surveys; mini piling -> site visits; subsidence repair -> subsidence surveys. If this company's own site consistently calls the first visit something else from the same family ('survey', 'site survey', 'site visit', 'assessment'), use the company's word and keep the trade noun from the table. NEVER the word 'inspection' or 'inspections' unless the company's own site uses that word — a UK homeowner books a survey, not an inspection. NEVER the word 'free'. NEVER 'estimate' or 'quote'. NEVER the whole business_type phrase inside this value.
instructions.inspection_singular: the singular of inspection_type, from the same table: damp survey, basement survey (structural and basement waterproofing both), site survey, structural survey, site visit, subsidence survey. It reads after 'a qualified, confirmed', so it must be one thing a homeowner books.
instructions.project_type: the OUTCOME NOUN the homeowner pays for, singular, homeowner wording, reading immediately before the word 'jobs'. By business_type: damp proofing -> treatment; structural waterproofing -> tanking; basement waterproofing -> waterproofing; underpinning -> underpinning; structural repairs -> repair; mini piling -> piling; subsidence repair -> repair. Never plural. Never a technical or trade-supplier term (say repair, not stabilisation; say tanking, not 'Type C cavity drainage'). Never 'project' or 'installation'.
instructions.city: ONLY if the 'city' known fact is blank: the UK town or city this company is based in, read from the website. Give the TOWN, never the county — 'Maidstone' not 'Kent', 'Solihull' not 'West Midlands', 'Bolton' not 'Greater Manchester' — and never a region ('the South East') or a service-area phrase ('covering Essex and London'). Use a county name ONLY when the site names no town at all. Otherwise repeat the known city exactly, with no trailing token of any kind.

rules: Decide business_type first — EXACTLY one of the seven allowed UK trades, the one the site leads with — then derive inspection_type, inspection_singular and project_type from the per-trade tables above; do not invent a fourth combination. The three trade values must agree with each other: business_type names the trade once, inspection_type is the first visit, project_type is the outcome the homeowner buys. No single word may appear in ALL THREE of business_type, inspection_type and project_type, and inspection_type must never contain the whole business_type phrase — those two are what `fill` reports as flag_word_used_3x and flag_visit_repeats_trade, and a flagged row is re-done. Never the word 'free' anywhere in inspection_type. UK spelling and UK vocabulary throughout. A damp firm does not get 'waterproofing' because the word appears somewhere on its site, and no company gets 'foundation repair'.

_r._: OPERATOR NOTES — not instructions to the personalisation subagent. They explain why each UK value differs from clients/atlas-growth/personalize-config.json (the US config) and what to watch in the fill report.
_r.template: Same shape and the same five placeholders as the US template, re-voiced for UK English. 'Noticed that you handle X' -> 'Noticed you do X around <town>' (how a UK trade would say it). The US offer line is kept but made to read naturally: 'We can book you 10 qualified damp surveys that turn into paid treatment jobs, in under 30 days.' 'There's no pay unless I book you...' is an American construction and becomes 'You only pay when I book you a qualified, confirmed damp survey.' No new placeholder was added — the second-email `company_short` variable is still an open item in STATE.md and is not introduced here.
_r.business_type: The allowed list is the UK trade vocabulary from ICP-uk.md, not the US one. 'foundation repair' is deliberately absent: ICP-uk.md records it as an American label that barely exists here, and this run's own universe self-labels as damp proofing / structural waterproofing (~60%), builders with a structural-repairs line (~17%), underpinning and piling (~8%), structural repair specialists (~8%). The seven values are the trades this run's 10 queries actually returned. The mapping line exists because two of the queries ('cellar tanking', 'wall tie replacement') have no matching business_type and would otherwise be invented by the reader: tanking lands on structural waterproofing, wall ties on structural repairs. The 174 damp-only leads should land on 'damp proofing' almost without exception.
_r.inspection_type: This is the biggest UK call in the file. In UK usage the first visit is a SURVEY, not an inspection and not an estimate: a damp firm does a damp survey, a structural or underpinning firm a structural or site survey, a piling firm a site visit. Using the US 'inspections'/'estimates' wording here is the single clearest tell that the email was written for another market, and 'free survey' is the exact phrase the whole UK trade already spams, so 'free' is banned outright (the engine also flags it as flag_free_in_visit). The per-trade table is chosen so that every row clears both live consistency flags: no word appears in all three values, and no inspection_type contains its whole business_type phrase. 'underpinning -> site surveys' and 'mini piling -> site visits' avoid a value that would swallow the trade phrase; 'structural waterproofing -> waterproofing surveys' pairs with 'tanking' as the outcome so that 'waterproofing' is used twice, never three times.
_r.inspection_singular: Straight singular of the table value, unchanged in method from the US config. It sits after 'a qualified, confirmed', so it has to be a single bookable thing — 'a qualified, confirmed damp survey' reads; 'a qualified, confirmed damp proofing' does not.
_r.project_type: The outcome noun a UK homeowner pays for, which is not always the trade noun. A homeowner buys damp TREATMENT, not 'damp proofing jobs'; buys TANKING from a structural waterproofing firm; buys WATERPROOFING from a basement specialist; buys UNDERPINNING, PILING or a REPAIR. 'treatment' is the UK-specific one worth defending: it is what the invoice says, and it keeps 'damp'/'proofing' from appearing a third time. structural waterproofing deliberately takes 'tanking' rather than 'waterproofing' — 'waterproofing' in all three values would trip flag_word_used_3x on every structural-waterproofing lead.
_r.city: UK towns, not counties. Google Maps and UK trade sites both hand back county and region names freely ('Kent', 'West Midlands', 'South East'), and 'around Kent' reads as an out-of-town agency wrote it. The county is allowed only when the site names no town at all. WATCH THIS ONE: this run is full of service-area listings with no address — SWEEP-PLAN.md counts 106 of the 377 unnamed leads with a blank city, and CH-REPORT.md found 207 leads whose full_address is entirely empty. The fallback is an empty string, which renders 'Noticed you do damp proofing around .' — broken copy, not a soft landing. Read `blank_city` in fill_report.json BEFORE upload and clear it the way the US run did, job-side: an `owner/city_overrides.json` in the run folder (the model's read of the site, else a keyless town-level reverse geocode, else leave the lead out of this send). Never fix it by editing the engine.
_r.rules: Same two-part discipline as the US rules line, stated against the flags the engine actually computes. Note what those flags are: `fill` reports flag_visit_repeats_trade (inspection_type contains the whole business_type string), flag_word_used_3x (one word appears three or more times across the three trade values), flag_free_in_visit (the word 'free' in inspection_type) and flag_outcome_off_trade. `redo` turns every flagged place_id into a higher-numbered batch whose values override on the next fill; loop fill -> redo -> one subagent -> fill until redo exits 2. The flags are the review — no eyeballing.
_r.context_cols: `state` is dropped from the US list. The UK has no state token: ICP-uk.md sets geo.region_from_city to null and READ-PLAN.md records that every source CSV in this run carries a blank state on purpose. Leaving it in the context list invites the reader to treat an empty field as missing data. `prep` still writes a (blank) state field into each batch item — that is the engine's fixed item shape and is not something to change for a job.
_r.engine_note_outcome_flag: KNOWN GAP, do not work around it in the config: build-plusvibe.js `fill` hardcodes its OUTCOME table with the US business_types only (foundation repair, basement waterproofing, crawl space repair, concrete leveling, house leveling, slab repair). For a UK business_type the lookup is undefined and the guard `if (OUTCOME[...] && ...)` short-circuits, so flag_outcome_off_trade CANNOT fire on this config — an off-trade outcome ('tanking jobs' for a mini piling firm) would ship silently. Only three of the four flags are live for the UK run. Mitigation for this run: the 7-lead test reads project_type by eye against business_type on every trade in the sample. The real fix is engine-side (read the outcome table from the config), needs operator approval and a test, and is drafted in the run's WRITEBACK-DRAFT.md.
_r.operator_2026-09-17: structural waterproofing visit noun changed from 'waterproofing surveys' to 'basement surveys' (operator, 3-lead test): the visit must not repeat a word of the trade phrase. Offer line approved as is.

_contact_name: OPERATOR NOTE — contact_name / salutation. Per the operator default, nothing here changes the name rule: a first and last name ride an address ONLY when the local part is built from that person's name (build-plusvibe.js `localOwns`; base writes name_basis=local_match, fill refuses to write on a violation, and `check --csv` re-applies it before upload). Role mailboxes — and this run is mostly info@ / enquiries@ / office@ — stay nameless whatever an upstream 'personal' tag says. A SEPARATE SALUTATION FALLBACK IS AN OPERATOR DECISION AND IS NOT SET HERE: the template opens with a bare 'Hi,' exactly as the US one does, and no {{first_name}} placeholder is introduced. Two UK-specific things to raise with the operator when that decision is made: (1) the engine's nickname table is US-shaped, so common UK pairs (Geoff/Geoffrey, Phil/Philip, Pete/Peter) do not resolve and those rows come out nameless — it fails safe, it does not mis-name; (2) HARVEST-REPORT.md found first-name mailboxes (jim@, jean@, garry@, paul@ at Falcon, Maljon, Atkins) that the upstream ranking scored below info@, so a named row may exist for a lead that currently carries a generic address — that is a ranking question for the waterfall, not a name-rule question.
_test_plan: OPERATOR NOTE — the gated test sequence, per google-maps-scrape SKILL STEP 7b ('The config is agreed with the operator on a 3-lead then a 7-lead test before the full set — every test surfaced a wording problem the previous one had not'). NOTHING IS FILLED AT FULL VOLUME UNTIL BOTH TESTS ARE SIGNED OFF. (1) THREE-LEAD TEST: hand-pick 3 leads that are already on three different business_types — one damp proofing, one underpinning or mini piling, one structural repairs or subsidence repair — run one subagent over a 3-item batch with skills/google-maps-scrape/personalize-subagent.md, and read the three finished `personalized_email` strings out loud to the operator. What is being checked is voice, not correctness: does 'damp surveys' / 'site visits' / 'treatment jobs' sound like a UK firm wrote it. (2) SEVEN-LEAD TEST: only after the 3-lead wording is agreed. Cover the remaining trades, include at least one damp-only-segment lead, one brand-family branch (Timberwise / Rentokil Property Care / Protectahome), one lead with a blank city, and one lead with no site text so the operator sees the fallback row as it will actually ship. Run `fill` on the 7 and read fill_report.json: expect 0 flag_visit_repeats_trade, 0 flag_word_used_3x, 0 flag_free_in_visit, and check project_type by eye on every trade because flag_outcome_off_trade cannot fire on this config (see _r.engine_note_outcome_flag). (3) FULL FILL: `prep` the rest, one Haiku subagent per batch, then fill -> redo -> subagent -> fill until `redo` exits 2, then `check --csv` on the finished upload. Report `fallback_only` and `blank_city` to the operator before any upload, exactly as the US run did. Every correction the redo prompts produce is written back INTO THIS FILE'S per-trade tables, so the next UK run's first pass flags stragglers, not batches.
